**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Religious Studies 3 (0785), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2019. Paper 3: The New Testament, Religion in Relation to Philosophy, Ethics and Morality, Historical Development of Islam (570CE-661CE). Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

The paper has six sections of six questions each: Section 2.1 The Gospel According to Luke (questions 1-6); Section 2.2 The Fourth Gospel (questions 7-12); Section 2.3 The Early Church as Reflected in Acts and 1 Corinthians (questions 13-18); Section 4.1 Philosophy of Religion (questions 19-24); Section 4.2 Ethics and Morality (questions 25-30); Section 6.0 The Historical Development of Islam (570CE - 661CE) (questions 31-36).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
With reference to Jesus' appearance to His disciples at Lake Tiberias (John 21); examine the importance of the resurrection appearances in the Fourth Gospel.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** In the Fourth Gospel the risen Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene (John 20:11-18), to the disciples in a locked room (John 20:19-23), to Thomas a week later (John 20:24-29), and finally at the Sea of Tiberias (John 21:1-14). The appearance by the lake, in a chapter that many scholars regard as an appendix added to the Gospel, contributes much to the overall meaning of the appearances.

**1. The appearance at Lake Tiberias (John 21).**
- Seven disciples go fishing at night and catch nothing. At daybreak Jesus stands on the shore and tells them to cast the net on the right side; the net is full of large fish, 153 in number (John 21:6-11).
- The beloved disciple recognises him ("It is the Lord!"), and Peter jumps into the water. Jesus has prepared bread and fish on a charcoal fire and invites them to breakfast (John 21:9-13).
- Jesus asks Peter three times "Do you love me?" and each time commissions him to feed his lambs and sheep (John 21:15-17). The threefold question answers the threefold denial, so Peter is forgiven and restored. Jesus foretells that Peter will die for his faith and calls him again to follow (John 21:18-19).
- The words about the beloved disciple clarify that he was not promised to live until the return of Jesus (John 21:20-23).

**2. The importance of the appearances in the Gospel as a whole.**
- *They prove the reality of the resurrection.* Jesus shows his hands and his side (John 20:20, 27), and he eats with the disciples (John 21:13). The body is real, although it is transformed, since he comes through closed doors.
- *They fulfil Jesus' promises.* In the Farewell Discourses he promised, "I will see you again and your hearts will rejoice" (John 16:22). The appearances bring peace and joy (John 20:19-21).
- *They lead to faith.* The disciples believe and Thomas confesses, "My Lord and my God!" Jesus then blesses those who have not seen and yet believe (John 20:28-29), the readers of the Gospel. This agrees with the stated aim of the Gospel in John 20:31.
- *They give the commission and the Spirit.* "As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you" and the gift of the Holy Spirit with the power to forgive sins are given in John 20:21-23. John 21 gives a pastoral commission to Peter.
- *They restore and unify the community.* Mary Magdalene becomes the first witness. The appearance to Peter restores a disciple who had failed, so that the church has a shepherd.
- *They prepare for the church's life.* The shared meal recalls the feeding in John 6 and the Eucharist, and the great catch of fish suggests the church's universal mission.

**Conclusion.** The appearances are the climax of the Gospel. The scene in John 21 completes them by showing forgiveness for Peter, a commission to care for the flock and the continuing presence of the risen Lord with his disciples at their daily work. Without the appearances, the Gospel would end in the sorrow of the cross; with them it ends with faith, mission and life.
